newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico luring retail banks to aid indebted farmers.
newsitem.headline: Mexico luring retail banks to aid indebted farmers.

text.p: The Mexican government is urging commercial banks to help credit-hungry farmers who say they have been neglected since the 1994 peso devaluation.
Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said on Tuesday the government plans to encourage retail banks to open branches in rural districts.

"One of our fundamental goals is to persuade the commercial banks to return to the agriculture sector. Since 1994 they have distanced themselves and the challenge is to have them return," Werner told agricultural leaders at the National Farm Council's (CNA) annual assembly.
Mexican farming leaders say their only credit option has been through government development banks, such as Banrural and Bancomext.
For 1997, about 55.234 billion pesos were set aside for farming credits, up 12 percent from 1996, Werner said.
Farmers say money is tight at harvest time, when they buy back crops from the government.

"We want to have more options, not just one -- the official Banco Rural. The commercial banks have little or no desire to help the countryside; they say it is bad business," Filiberto Cruz Leyva, president of the agriculture confederation in Sonora state, told Reuters.

He said that government credits and exporting aid took the place of commercial banks, when the commercial banks' countryside credit support disappeared in the crisis that followed the 1994 peso devaluation. Government development banks shoulder at least 80 percent of agriculture credits.
Mexico's government has a history of bearing farmers' burdens, even subsidizing seed prices and irrigation costs.

Werner said that income from state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) exports this year would go to support the countryside. He declined to say how much they would get, but media reports placed it at $1 billion.
Despite the millions earmarked for helping farmers, agricultural leaders complained that the credits are poorly administered.
"They are not well-organized, not getting to where they are needed," said an agricultural leader who declined to be named.
Grain farmers are especially needy because of lower international prices and a more agressive planting program.

"We've had to spend more than we expected. We've increased the area for planting, but now we need more funding because of the drop in international prices," Agriculture Minister Francisco Labastida said earlier this week.

The Mexican government boosted its 1997 aid to grain farmers to 3.5 billion pesos from a previously alloted 500 million pesos. The sugar industry has also called for government support to relieve a debt burden running to billions of pesos.
